T6.7. The two curve pairs drawn in the main-text Fig. 3, in physical values. Case (a): zero-based test indices 2890 / 5067, database Sample_ID 141475 / 71905. Case (b): zero-based test indices 500 / 4560, Sample_ID 37892 / 87198. The indices are positions in the frozen test array; the Sample_ID values identify the same two curves in the source database. The two tables per case give the nine parameters in physical units and the six paired coordinates in physical log₁₀ units, where the shared scale a = (log₁₀θₙ + log₁₀θₚ)/2 is the logarithm of the geometric mean of the two carrier parameters of a family and r = log₁₀(θₙ/θₚ) is their difference in log₁₀. The per-parameter difference in the two parameter tables is the absolute difference of the two physical log₁₀ values, |Δlog₁₀θ| = |log₁₀θᵢ − log₁₀θⱼ| = |log₁₀(θᵢ/θⱼ)|, and the factor column is 10^|Δlog₁₀θ|, that is the larger of the two physical values divided by the smaller. No factor in this subsection is formed from baseline-normalized or otherwise rescaled parameter differences. The same values at full source precision are in si_table_s6_7_figure_cases.csv and si_table_s6_7_figure_case_coordinates.csv.

Selection rule, applied to the corrected undirected pair set. Restrict to the closest 1% of pairs by ascending d_J (n = 112 of 11,245 pairs); take the pair with the largest absolute mobility log-ratio difference |Δr| as case (a); then, from the same tier with case (a)'s pair removed, take the pair with the largest absolute bulk-lifetime log-ratio difference |Δr| as case (b). The measured values are |Δr| = 1.354456 for case (a) and |Δr| = 1.266201 for case (b). Both picks are also the largest in the same tier when the coordinate is normalized by its random-pair baseline (T6.9), because dividing a coordinate by one fixed positive constant does not change the ordering. Ties would be broken by position in the tier ordering, that is by smaller d_J first. The tier restriction is load-bearing: the largest |Δr| for mobility over all 11,245 corrected pairs is 1.361187 and belongs to pair 3396 / 13213, which is not drawn in Fig. 3.

T6.8. Distance-tier comparison of the six paired coordinates. Columns after the first give all corrected undirected pairs and then the closest 10%, 5%, 1%, 0.5% and 0.1% of those pairs, taken in ascending d_J. Column headers give the tier as the fraction of all corrected pairs it holds. The tier sizes are 11,245, 1,124, 562, 112, 56, 11 pairs, so the three smallest sets hold 112, 56 and 11 pairs and their medians are correspondingly less stable. "Pairs" counts the curve pairs in a set and "Distinct curves" the test curves that appear in it; values are absolute coordinate differences divided by the random-pair median of the same coordinate (T6.9), so one is the random-pair level. The interquartile range describes the spread of the paired differences within the set and is not a confidence interval; pairs share test curves, so they are not independent observations, and no p-value is reported for any set. Dividing a coordinate by a fixed positive baseline changes the scale of the numbers but not their ordering, so the raw differences rank the sets in the same order. A median close to the random-pair level is reported as a value, and nothing further is inferred from it.

T6.9. Random-pair baselines of the six paired coordinates. Each value is the median absolute difference of that coordinate over the random-pair baseline used throughout this work: 200,000 ordered index pairs drawn uniformly from the 15,307 test curves with numpy.random.default_rng(42), self-pairs dropped, 199,985 retained. These six constants normalize the coordinate differences in T6.7 and T6.8, in Fig. 3c and in Fig. S7. Differences of physical log₁₀ values are independent of the unit basis of the underlying parameters, so the baselines are too.
